hook: A transit agency asks random samples of city and suburban residents whether they would ride a new train line: 62% of 400 city residents say yes, and 54% of 300 suburban residents do. The gap in the samples is 8 percentage points. But how big is the gap for everyone in the region? A confidence interval for the difference gives a range of plausible values.

prereq.q: What critical value $z^*$ goes with 95% confidence?
prereq.why: 95% in the middle leaves 2.5% in each tail; $z^* = 1.96$.

prereq.q: For independent samples, the standard deviation of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is found by
options: adding the two variances, then taking the square root

figure.caption: The 95% interval for $p_{\text{city}} - p_{\text{sub}}$: the sample difference 0.08 plus or minus a margin of error of 0.074.

chain.cause: You want the true difference $p_1 - p_2$ but only have two samples
chain.effect: the sample difference $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is the point estimate

chain.cause: Sample differences vary with standard deviation $\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}$
chain.effect: replace each $p$ by its $\hat{p}$ to get the standard error, since the $p$s are unknown

chain.cause: The sampling distribution is approximately normal when the four counts reach 10
chain.effect: go $z^*$ standard errors each way: $(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$

chain.cause: The method captures the true difference in about 95% of samples
chain.effect: say "we are 95% confident that the interval captures the true difference in proportions", naming the order of subtraction

ideas: Conditions: two independent random samples or two randomly assigned groups; each sample under 10% of its population; at least 10 successes and 10 failures in each sample.
Interpret: "We are 95% confident that the interval from ... to ... captures the true difference in the proportions of ... (group 1 minus group 2)."
Random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; random sampling allows generalizing to the populations.

misconception.wrong: A 95% interval for $p_1 - p_2$ means 95% of the people in group 1 are that much more likely to say yes.
misconception.right: The interval estimates one number, the true difference in the two population proportions. It says nothing about individuals; the 95% describes how often the method captures that number.

summary: To estimate $p_1 - p_2$, use the two-sample z interval $(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$ after checking random, 10% and large counts for each sample. Interpret it as capturing the true difference in proportions, in context and with the order of subtraction named.
